headline: The evidence base
punch: And only one of them measured whether anyone actually ended up taller.

headline: Aromatase inhibitors
body: As the established way to delay fusion and gain height. The confidence in how people talk about them is not matched by the literature behind them.
punch: A systematic review went looking for the trials.

headline: It found four
body: 207 participants total. 84 actually on the active drug. In male children and adolescents with short stature, versus placebo.
punch: That's the entire randomised evidence base.

headline: All four
body: Predicted adult height went up in every trial. Which sounds like the answer until you notice what predicted adult height actually is.
punch: A model's output. Not a measured person.

headline: Only one trial
body: One study followed participants to actual near-final adult height — and it did so under non-randomised extension conditions, not as a controlled comparison.
punch: Three of the four never checked whether it worked.

headline: And that one trial
body: No meaningful difference in final adult height. The one time anyone measured the outcome that matters, the effect didn't appear.
punch: Predicted height went up. Actual height didn't.

headline: This is the gap
body: Predicted adult height is a surrogate endpoint. Surrogates are useful for shortening trials and famously unreliable for telling you the treatment worked.
punch: Ask whether a study measured the thing or a proxy for the thing.

headline: The honest position
body: Mechanistically well grounded, clinically used, and the randomised evidence for adult height gain is thin and does not yet demonstrate the benefit.
punch: Plausible and unproven are allowed to coexist.
